New CEO for ESKOM: In search of a unicorn

By: Joy Summers | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The single biggest risk to South Africa is Eskom, says Finance Minister Tito Mboweni. Now the race is on to find a new CEO, but who will have the courage and what qualities will be needed

Unique Selling Point:
Candid admissions from the Key Eskom players on Camera and hopefully an interview with Grant Pattison about being a CEO in troubled times

Summary:
It’s that time. AGAIN. – Eskom is in search of a new CEO. But we might as well be looking for a unicorn. Since 1994 Eskom has had 12 CEO’s. Some of them have tried, others have been incompetent, and half of them have been tainted by allegations of corruption. None of those implicated have been charged, even as they brought this once proud utility to its knees.
The last CEO Phakamani Hadebe walked away from a packed results presentation with a final quote from Frederick Douglass:
“It is not light that we need, but fire; it is not the gentle shower, but thunder. We need the storm, the whirlwind, and the earthquake.” He said and walked away.


Further information:
While the board has tinkered around the edges of the problem, political interference prevented the former CEO from doing what he knew Eskom needed. Its two biggest costs are its people, its coal and fuel for generation. But he could do little about either.

With 15 000 staff too many more than necessary, Phakamani knew he needed to slim down, but a president faced with an election, said no way Hose, so instead Eskom had to find other ways to save money.

Immediately they set about shaving R10 billion in costs. They managed R9.9 billion rand, but when their power stations failed, out came the Open cycle gas turbines costing them R6 billion on diesel, which pretty much wiped out their savings.

“Eskom is running out of runway” said the Chief Financial Officer as he presented a miserable set of results. Without government support Eskom is not a going concern he told the audience. That government support is substantial – R230 billion over the next ten years, but even that is not enough, which forced the Finance Minister to give them another R59 billion just to keep the lights on.

The numbers are staggering – R20 billion loss for the last financial year, R440 billion in debt and not enough money coming in to even pay the interest.

“Eskom is in a death spiral” admitted Hadebe.

We will only be sustainable if we can halve that number the CFO, told investors and journalists last week. But that is looking increasingly unlikely. Eskom’s reputation is shot, even the Chinese don’t want to lend them any more money. Municipalities across the country owe them R38 billion rand and the only way they can plug the hole is to get NERSA to agree to give them an increase in electricity tariffs. But as South Africans get poorer and find themselves unemployed, it’s unlikely that NERSA will give Eskom the 50% increase they require, so it looks like Eskom may take NERSA to court. No wonder the last CEO couldn’t sleep at night.

In a candid public admission he said that when he arrived he sat with the board and they couldn’t understand how it was possible that an entity that had received a 385% tariff increase in ten years -against an inflation rate of 6% - and an R85 billion rand bailout, could be in such a position.

Now, it’s not his problem as he takes himself off for much needed R and R and the desperate search for another CEO begins.

“They need a statesman in that position” says former Board spokesman Khulani Quoma, “ someone who doesn’t get excited when the president phones. Someone whose already achieved what they need to do and isn’t intimidated.

But strangely and perhaps an indication of just how slow Eskom is to respond, the board waited 68 days before beginning the search not for a new CEO, but for a company that could find them a new CEO.

Former Eskom spokesperson has also left and gave himself 3 months to recover. He has lived through 6 CEO’s at Eskom and seen the good, the bad and the ugly. He suggests the only way to find a new leader for Eskom is to embark on an open selection process like one does with judges.

Eskom is getting more and more complicated says Khaya Sithole. They may be able to keep the lights on for a few more months but perhaps they should just give us the co- ordinates for Christine Lagarde and the IMF instead. He says. “And what about the conflict of interest of the chairman Jabu Mabuza put in place until October as a place holder.

Mabuza himself has interests in the Mzimkhulu Mine

And what kind of qualities and skills will that person need. Can one man even do the job? Carte Blanche asks a CEO of a major private company what he did to take it back from the brink and what Eskom needs to save not only itself but the country

FINAL SCRIPT ESKOM’S TOP JOB TX 18th August 2019 Commentary One Phakamani Hadebe, the man who turned around the landbank, has been defeated by Eskom. At the end of July, 18 months into the job, he said goodbye to his colleagues, investors, labour, and journalists at Eskom’s results Phakamani Hadebe Let me leave you with a quote which I think exemplifies an occasion of this sort, and what Eskom needs: For it is not the light that is needed, but fire. It is not the gentle shower but thunder. We need a storm, and we need earthquake and that is what Eskom needs Commentary Two Fire and Thunder, a storm and an earthquake – strong words from the outgoing CEO. We should listen, says commentator, Khaya Sithole Khaya he is saying that the matter is very urgent – and I think that sense of urgency is missing in a lot of the political decision makers, it is quite remarkable that having resigned at the end of May, he stepped out at the end of July, and the process of finding a CEO was only started that particular week. The question that has to be asked is what the hell was the board thinking, what was their plan, do they not think this is a crisis? LINK The numbers are dire, the chief financial officer suggested that Eskom is running out of runway and has admitted that without the big bailouts the utility would not be a going concern Commentary three This year Eskom recorded a R20 billion loss. Its debt sits at R440 billion rand. Customers aren’t paying, and Eskom can’t even afford the interest payments on their debt, which is why Hadebe wanted to freeze wage increases to save money Khaya Sithole Phakamani Hadebe says last year I will freeze wages because I don’t have the money, the politicians come in and say you will do no such thing, you will cost us votes and we have a general election coming up do you have anyone who will say I am going to put up with that type of interference, that type of nonsense? I don’t think so! Commentary Four Now the hunt is on for a new CEO, but its last chance saloon here at Megawatt Park. Since 1994 12 CEO’s have come and gone. But this time Eskom’s debt hangs like a dark cloud over the economy. So, who is up for that challenge? Grant Pattison Let me just say on behalf of professional CEO’s, I think the absolute non-negotiable is that Eskom has to be depoliticized Commentary Five If you’re looking for a brave CEO, Grant Pattison fits the bill, but he is not interested in the Eskom job, because he has his hands full saving EDCON, and that has given him a unique perspective Grant I think all political parties need to come together and agree to depolitisize this, agree it’s a national project in the national interest and rally all citizens, the whole country behind this really brave CEO. Commentary Six Pattison has just pulled Edcon from the brink and saved 100 000 jobs. There are similarities between the two, he says Grant Both were in the recent past, really great organisations, that have been messed up by the shareholder and the leadership. I think those are what they have in common. There is a two nought difference – you take Edcon size problem, you add two noughts onto it, and it somewhat looks like Eskom Commentary Seven Pattison closed about 150 stores, he gave shares to the UIF, he convinced landlords to inject money into the company -even the unions came on board. Grant I think the greatest challenge of all was trying to get everyone to accept the reality of the situation we found ourselves in MASA But then somebody needs to make tough decisions? Grant Yes, and how does one get past a tough decision, first of all we need to get over our collective denial. It only looks difficult because we are in denial. That is what creates a difficult decision – once everyone gets around the table and says we all have to give up, we all have to lose here – then these decisions don’t look so difficult because I think they are rather obvious by the way I don’t think it’s actually that complicated. Commentary eight Already Eskom has cleaned up governance, and embarked on cost saving measures. But its not nearly enough and the tough decisions have been put off at Eskom. Instead the state keeps throwing money at it. R289 billion and counting. Grant Pattison Well certainly in Edcon we had to separate the two problems. You have the operating problem of the company, how to run it profitably and then you have the historical financial debt problem. They are two separate things, both are solvable, but really the financial problem is mostly solved by the debt going away. Commentary Nine He says Eskom’s debt must be treated separately. Grant I don’t think there is any question that operationally Eskom can be fixed. That must be possible, we have been generating power for 100 years, not that tricky as an engineering challenge so its definitely fixable. The financial side different matter – mostly got to get rid of the debt – at some point the debt holders need to either be repaid through some form or walk away from the debt Commentary ten Politicians have been kicking around Eskom’s R440 billion debt for months. Perhaps its denial that is paralyzing decision making. GRANT You are somewhat dependent on the quality of the leadership around you. You know a leader can make a difference, something that looks completely impossible and destined to fail can be changed just by a single person being able to take the right perspective so I think that is part of depoliticizing Eskom and getting everyone committed to its savior – and then realizing that the ultimate solution has to hurt everyone equally. Commentary eleven It’s not just the CEO’s that have taken strain. Former Eskom spokesman Khulu Pasiwe says he was an absent father for years, as he fielded questions from journalists from 5am to midnight. Three months ago, he resigned Masa Kekana How many CEO did you outlast? Khulu I joined Eskom in 2008 in the ten- year period I think we had 11 CEO That is a lot? Khulu That is a lot in fact in one year I think around 2017 we had three different CEO’s, the rationale from was that they needed to rotate them so people could get exposure and things like that Commentary twelve It’s time now to choose the CEO differently he says. Khulu Pasiwe In many cases the processes are very opaque, in some cases you just hear so and so appointed and that is it. Maybe one of the ways we can avoid this particular problem, is to open the process up so it becomes similar to the process of appointing judges. The public may not have input but at least they can watch this thing on tv – they can follow. So, the whole process is transparent Commentary thirteen Pattison thinks that would scare of potentially good CEO’s Pattison I think it’s essential but I still place my one precondition before that happens, is that it has to be depoliticized, because let’s say you ask me the question would I be prepared to go to a public interview and have every political and interested body – asking every single difficult question they could, the answer would be no, why would I do that? Commentary fourteen This week it was reported that two former Eskom executives have put their names in the hat – But Eskom has until October before it makes a final decision. In the meantime, chairman Jabu Mabuza is holding the fort. JABU MABUZA I have availed myself to be a placeholder for the next three months. I do this being mindful of the need for leadership stability. Certainly not a job I would have applied for. I guess I have a conflict of interest in that I love my country more than perhaps I love myself LINK MASA but this didn’t go down well with the unions who are already calling for his head – one of their complaints is his conflict of interests Commentary fifteen Mabuza is a director of forty- five other companies including Eskom. His conflicts of interest although publicly declared, sit uncomfortably with the unions. In February he told the Zondo commission that his family has a joint interest in mining, an interest is represented by his son Lwazi. This is the mine Mzimkulu, which has supplied Eskom with coal. Mabuza also declared that he has resigned as chairman of a holding company that owns companies that do a third of Eskom’s boiler repairs. He says he has placed his interests in a blind trust. Mabuza declined an interview KHAYA SITHOLE The context that applies to Eskom is that most of the people that have been found wanting are people who very much so are accused of having particular conflicts of interest. If you look Matshela Koko and the question of Impulse for example. Then it’s brings the question is do you believe it’s ideal for the chairman who is part of the clean sweep to have similar conflicts of interest Commentary Sixteen Now as Eskom risks bringing the country down with it -the urgency of finding the right CEO quickly becomes critical. Masa Take me through the journey, this seems like a really tough job? Grant Yes, it is very personal and its quite hard to deal with personal challenge while you are in the public eye. You’re largely expected to be invincible, / and that is why you need a really good team and board and ministers to help you through that process

The last CEO Phakamani Hadebe walked away from a packed results presentation with a final quote from Frederick Douglass: “It is not light that we need, but fire; it is not the gentle shower, but thunder. We need the storm, the whirlwind, and the earthquake.” He said and walked away.
metadata.Further information: While the board has tinkered around the edges of the problem, political interference prevented the former CEO from doing what he knew Eskom needed. Its two biggest costs are its people, its coal and fuel for generation. But he could do little about either. With 15 000 staff too many more than necessary, Phakamani knew he needed to slim down, but a president faced with an election, said no way Hose, so instead Eskom had to find other ways to save money. Immediately they set about shaving R10 billion in costs. They managed R9.9 billion rand, but when their power stations failed, out came the Open cycle gas turbines costing them R6 billion on diesel, which pretty much wiped out their savings. “Eskom is running out of runway” said the Chief Financial Officer as he presented a miserable set of results. Without government support Eskom is not a going concern he told the audience. That government support is substantial – R230 billion over the next ten years, but even that is not enough, which forced the Finance Minister to give them another R59 billion just to keep the lights on. The numbers are staggering – R20 billion loss for the last financial year, R440 billion in debt and not enough money coming in to even pay the interest. “Eskom is in a death spiral” admitted Hadebe. We will only be sustainable if we can halve that number the CFO, told investors and journalists last week. But that is looking increasingly unlikely. Eskom’s reputation is shot, even the Chinese don’t want to lend them any more money. Municipalities across the country owe them R38 billion rand and the only way they can plug the hole is to get NERSA to agree to give them an increase in electricity tariffs. But as South Africans get poorer and find themselves unemployed, it’s unlikely that NERSA will give Eskom the 50% increase they require, so it looks like Eskom may take NERSA to court. No wonder the last CEO couldn’t sleep at night. In a candid public admission he said that when he arrived he sat with the board and they couldn’t understand how it was possible that an entity that had received a 385% tariff increase in ten years -against an inflation rate of 6% - and an R85 billion rand bailout, could be in such a position. Now, it’s not his problem as he takes himself off for much needed R and R and the desperate search for another CEO begins. “They need a statesman in that position” says former Board spokesman Khulani Quoma, “ someone who doesn’t get excited when the president phones. Someone whose already achieved what they need to do and isn’t intimidated. But strangely and perhaps an indication of just how slow Eskom is to respond, the board waited 68 days before beginning the search not for a new CEO, but for a company that could find them a new CEO. Former Eskom spokesperson has also left and gave himself 3 months to recover. He has lived through 6 CEO’s at Eskom and seen the good, the bad and the ugly. He suggests the only way to find a new leader for Eskom is to embark on an open selection process like one does with judges. Eskom is getting more and more complicated says Khaya Sithole. They may be able to keep the lights on for a few more months but perhaps they should just give us the co- ordinates for Christine Lagarde and the IMF instead. He says. “And what about the conflict of interest of the chairman Jabu Mabuza put in place until October as a place holder. Mabuza himself has interests in the Mzimkhulu Mine And what kind of qualities and skills will that person need. Can one man even do the job? Carte Blanche asks a CEO of a major private company what he did to take it back from the brink and what Eskom needs to save not only itself but the country
